title: Architecture & Standards: API, Coding, Infra, Model-Serving, Observability, Performance, and ADRs
author: Ava Chen
content:
Summary
This page consolidates Redwood Inference's canonical architecture and engineering standards across API design, coding practices, infrastructure, model-serving, observability, performance targets, and ADR (Architectural Decision Record) process. The goal is to provide a single, actionable reference that teams can follow to deliver consistent, secure, and observable services that meet our reliability and cost objectives.

Scope
Applies to all new services, service-level changes, and model onboarding work across Hosted, Dedicated, and Private deployment modes. Exceptions must be captured via an ADR and approved by the relevant owners.

Principles
- Developer-first: APIs and infra should minimize friction for engineers and customers.
- Production-grade: defaults prioritize operability, security, and cost-effectiveness.
- Observable-by-default: every service ships metrics, traces, and logs.
- Reproducible infra: infrastructure is managed via code (Terraform) and peer-reviewed.
- Incremental decisions: use ADRs for non-trivial architectural choices.

Ownership and Contacts
- Standards owner: Architecture & Standards guild (eng-platform).
- Runtime & model-serving: eng-serving-runtime (owners: Marcus Li, Priya Kumar).
- Infra & provisioning: eng-infra (owners: Diego Morales).
- Observability & SRE: eng-sre (owners: Lena Hofmann).
- Security review: security-and-compliance.

1) API Standards
Purpose: Ensure consistent, versioned, secure, and well-documented APIs across products.
Key Requirements:
- API style: REST-first for external public APIs; gRPC or internal HTTP/JSON for high-throughput internal services. Follow OpenAPI 3.0 for REST endpoints.
- Versioning: Major version in path (e.g., /v1/...), semver for implementations. Backwards-incompatible changes require an ADR and a deprecation plan (minimum 90 days for public APIs).
- Authentication & Authorization: Use JWT-based tokens for public APIs and mTLS or internal IAM for service-to-service communication. All endpoints must validate caller identity and enforce least privilege.
- Contracts & Schemas: Provide OpenAPI spec stored in repo at /api/openapi.yaml and published to internal API registry. Use JSON Schema for request/response validation.
- Error model: Use structured errors with HTTP status codes and machine-readable error codes. Example: {"error": {"code": "quota_exceeded", "message": "Rate limit exceeded", "request_id": "..."}}
- Rate limiting: Default rate limit policy enforced at API gateway; per-customer overrides configured via product config. Document expected quotas in product docs.
- Pagination & Streaming: Use cursor-based pagination for list endpoints. For streaming responses (generation), support chunked transfer/HTTP2 streaming and well-documented end-of-stream markers.
- Observability hooks: All public endpoints must emit metrics: request_count, request_latency_ms (histogram), request_errors. Logs must include request_id and auth_identity.
- API review checklist (PR required): OpenAPI spec present, schema validation, auth enforced, error model correct, example requests/responses, migration/deprecation plan if applicable.

API contract example (OpenAPI snippet):
POST /v1/generate
Request: content-type: application/json
{"model": "redwood-1-small", "input": "...", "max_tokens": 128}
Response 200:
{"request_id": "req_xxx", "tokens": ["Hello", "world"]}

2) Coding Standards
Purpose: Maintain consistent, readable, and testable code across repos.
Language & Style:
- Primary languages: Go for core runtime services, Python for orchestration and ML tooling, TypeScript for front-end and console services.
- Formatting: Enforce gofmt/golangci-lint for Go, black/ruff for Python, and eslint/prettier for TypeScript.
- Linting & Static Analysis: CI must run linters and block merges on high/critical issues. Use language-specific linters configured in repo-level CI.
Testing:
- Unit tests: Target >= 80% coverage for new modules and components; critical path code should aim for 90%+ coverage.
- Integration tests: Include deterministic integration tests that run in CI with mocked external dependencies.
- Load and perf tests: Benchmark-critical services must include reproducible performance tests checked into repository under /bench.
Code Review & PRs:
- All changes require at least one approving reviewer (two for infra, security-sensitive, or major changes).
- PRs must include a clear description, testing notes, and rollout/rollback plan when applicable.
Secrets & Keys:
- Never store secrets in code. Use vault integration (HashiCorp Vault / KMS) and reference secrets via env vars or secrets manager.

3) Infrastructure Standards
Provisioning & IaC:
- All cloud resources must be provisioned via Terraform modules (gitops model). Repositories must use our standard module registry and naming conventions.
- Environment parity: staging must be a scaled-down replica of production (networking, IAM, and observability).
- Tagging policy: every resource must have tags: project, owner, cost_center, environment.
Network & Security:
- VPC design: private subnets for compute; NAT for outbound where required; strict egress policies.
- Encryption: at-rest encryption using provider KMS; in-transit: TLS 1.2+ and mTLS for sensitive links.
- IAM: principle of least privilege; use temporary creds and short-lived tokens.
Deployment & Releases:
- Blue/green or canary deployments recommended for services serving production traffic.
- Automated rollback triggers: if deployment causes SLO violation or critical alerts within the observation window, trigger rollback.
Capacity & Cost Controls:
- Autoscaling rules should be tied to business metrics (e.g., RPS, tokens/sec) and capped by predicted cost windows.
- Reserved capacity (Dedicated) follows separate governance: capacity planning doc must be attached to any Dedicated-related Terraform change.

4) Model-Serving Standards
Purpose: Ensure models are served reproducibly, safely, and efficiently across Hosted/Dedicated/Private modes.
Model Onboarding Checklist:
- Model card: owner, architecture, intended tasks, training data (high-level), limitations. 
- Quantization profile: supported bitwidths and expected memory/perf tradeoffs.
- Compatibility matrix: supported sequence lengths, kv-cache behavior, attention types.
- Eval harness results: baseline prompts, quality metrics (ROUGE, BLEU, human eval summary), and regression thresholds.
Versioning & Rollouts:
- Model artifacts: store in immutable object storage with digest (sha256). Model versions follow semver-like tags: model-name@vYYYYMMDD-<build>.
- Rollouts: use canary (5–10% traffic) with automated quality checks (latency, error rate, quality regressions on held-out prompt set).
- Fallbacks: define fallback model variants for graceful degradation (smaller quantized model or different region).
Runtime Configurations:
- Batching & KV-caching: default batch window 8ms for latency-sensitive routes; runtime can increase batching for cost-oriented endpoints per route config.
- Memory/Perf profiles: publish kernel and cudnn configs tested per GPU type.
- Safety & Guardrails: include soft-blocking filters at model gateway and downstream deterministic post-filters where required by customer.

Model-serving example config (route-level):
route: /v1/generate
model: redwood-1-large@20260110-a1b2c3
batching: {"strategy": "auto", "max_batch_size": 32, "latency_target_ms": 50}
kv_cache: enabled
quantization_profile: int8
quality_checks: /eval/promptset/production-sanity.v1

5) Observability Standards
Purpose: Ensure teams can detect, triage, and resolve incidents quickly and measure user-facing quality.
Metrics:
- Metric naming convention: service.<service_name>.<operation>.<metric> (e.g., service.runtime.generate.request_latency_ms).
- Required metrics per service: request_count, request_latency_ms (histogram), error_count, tokens_generated, model_load_time_ms.
- Percentiles: ingest p50/p90/p95/p99 histograms for request latency.
Tracing & Logs:
- Distributed traces: instrument entry points and significant downstream calls. Propagate request_id and trace_id.
- Structured logs: JSON lines with fields: timestamp, level, service, request_id, trace_id, user_id (if available), message, metadata.
Dashboards & Alerts:
- Dashboards: every service must have a compute dashboard (CPU/GPU usage, memory, queue depth), and an SLO dashboard (latency percentiles, error rates, traffic).
- Alerting: define page/SEV (pager/SLACK) routing. Alerts must be actionable with clear runbook links.
- Alert thresholds (examples):
  - SEV 1 (pager): P95 latency increase > 2x baseline AND error_rate > 1% sustained for 2 minutes.
  - SEV 2 (slack + oncall): error_rate > 5% for 10 minutes or sustained queue depth > 80% of buffer.
Logging retention:
- Production logs: 30 days hot, 90 days cold; sensitive logs may have reduced retention and must follow security retention policy.

6) Performance Standards & Benchmarks
SLO Structure:
- SLOs must be defined for external and key internal APIs. Each SLO document must include objective, measurement window, and owner.
- Example SLOs for Hosted text-generation (default route, <= 128 tokens):
  - Availability: 99.95% (measured as successful responses excluding planned maintenance) over 30-day window.
  - Latency: P95 < 250 ms, P99 < 750 ms.
  - Error rate: < 0.5% (4xx excluded where appropriate)
- For long-running / large-token jobs, define separate SLO tiers (e.g., batch-generation P95 < 2s per 1k tokens).
Benchmarking & Perf Suite:
- Benchmarking repo: eng-serving-runtime/benchmark-suite stores perf harnesses and reproducible scripts.
- Baseline reports: every major runtime change must include before/after perf artifacts and a short analysis summarizing token/sec, latency distribution, and GPU utilization.
Load Testing:
- Use synthetic workloads that mimic token distributions observed in production (histogram provided by eng-sre).
- Run load tests as part of release gating for runtime, infra, and model-serving changes that touch critical paths.
Tail-latency & Cost Controls:
- Tail-latency budgets are part of the SLO and must be evaluated per-model. If a change increases P99 by > 10% while cost decreases, an ADR is required to accept the tradeoff.

7) Architectural Decision Records (ADRs)
Purpose: Capture and rationalize non-trivial architecture decisions so they can be reviewed, audited, and revisited.
Process:
1. When a decision affects cross-team compatibility, long-lived design, or has measurable cost/security implications, create an ADR before implementation.
2. ADR must be peer-reviewed and include: context, alternatives considered, decision, consequences, owners, and migration/deprecation plan.
3. Store ADRs in the architecture repo under /docs/adrs with filename: NN-title-short.md (incrementing number).
4. Link ADR to related PRs and Confluence pages.
ADR template (summary):
- Title: Short descriptive title
- Status: proposed | accepted | superseded | deprecated
- Context: Why is this decision needed?
- Decision: What is the chosen approach?
- Alternatives: What other options were considered?
- Consequences: Migration plan, rollback, operational considerations, cost/security impact.
- Date & Authors: who signed off
Example ADR topics:
- Migration to a single OpenAPI gateway vs per-team gateways
- Choice of quantization library for int8 inference
- Default batching strategy for low-latency routes

8) Change Management & Release Checklist
Before merging a change that affects production behavior, ensure the following (checklist):
- [ ] Design review completed (if scope > minor bug).
- [ ] ADR created/updated for architectural-impacting changes.
- [ ] Tests: unit, integration, and perf tests added/passing.
- [ ] OpenAPI/schema updated and published.
- [ ] Monitoring: metrics, traces, logs instrumented; dashboards updated.
- [ ] Rollout plan: canary configuration, success criteria, rollback triggers.
- [ ] Security review completed for sensitive changes.

9) Enforcement and Exceptions
- Enforcement: Repos are scanned in CI for compliance with mandatory checks (linters, schema validation, required metrics). Non-compliant PRs will block merge.
- Exceptions: to deviate from these standards, file an ADR that documents the rationale, compensating controls, and an expiration/reevaluation date.

Appendix A — ADR Template (markdown-friendly)
# ADR NN: Title
Status: proposed
Date: YYYY-MM-DD
## Context
...
## Decision
...
## Alternatives
...
## Consequences
...
## Owners
...

Appendix B — Example Alert Rules (prometheus-style, pseudo YAML)
- alert: RuntimeHighP95Latency
  expr: histogram_quantile(0.95, rate(service_runtime_request_latency_ms_bucket[2m])) > 0.5
  for: 2m
  labels: { severity: pager }
  annotations: { runbook: "/confluence/eng-sre/runbooks/runtime-high-p95" }

- alert: ModelLoadFailureRate
  expr: increase(model_load_errors_total[5m]) / increase(model_load_attempts_total[5m]) > 0.02
  for: 5m
  labels: { severity: page }
